blocks.text: Avalanche vs snowball

Two valid strategies. Avalanche: minimums on everything, every spare dollar at the HIGHEST RATE first. Mathematically optimal. Snowball: spare dollars at the SMALLEST BALANCE first. Psychologically optimal, because closed accounts feel like wins and wins keep you going. The best strategy is the one you'll still be running in month eight. If motivation is fragile, snowball; if you're a spreadsheet person, avalanche.

blocks.title: Real talk
blocks.text: Minimum payments are designed to keep you paying for decades: on a typical card balance, minimums alone can take 20+ years and double what you borrowed. The minimum is the floor that prevents damage, never the plan.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: Arun has: Card A $3,200 at 24%, Card B $900 at 19%, student loan $18,000 at 4.5%. One page, sorted. Plan: minimums on everything; $400 extra to Card B first (snowball: dead in 10 weeks, one account gone), then the $400+Card B's minimum onto Card A. The student loan stays on minimums; at 4.5%, his spare dollars will eventually do better in an index fund. Eleven months to card-free.
Two calls worth making

First: call the card company and ask for a lower rate: "I've been a customer three years, always on time; can you reduce my APR?" It works more often than anyone believes. Second: if your credit improved since the debt began, look at a balance transfer (0% intro windows) or consolidation. Moving 24% debt to 0% for 15 months is a legal cheat code, IF you don't use the freed-up card to dig again.

blocks.caption: how long minimum payments can stretch a single card balance. The minimum is the floor, not the plan.

quiz.q: The first strategic move against debt is…
options: Put every spare dollar at it starting with this paycheck
Every balance, every rate and every minimum on one page
Consolidate it all into a single monthly payment
Close the cards so the balances cannot grow again
quiz.explain: Strategy requires visibility. The ten-minute list is the boring act of courage everything else builds on.

quiz.q: Avalanche vs snowball. The honest answer for most people:
options: Avalanche every time, because the arithmetic decides it
Snowball every time, because momentum is what carries it
Whichever one you will still be running in month eight
Neither: the difference between them is mostly marketing
quiz.explain: Avalanche is optimal on paper; abandoned avalanche is worth zero. Consistency beats optimality.

quiz.q: You have a 4.5% student loan and a 24% card. Spare dollars go…
options: Split them evenly, so both balances keep moving down
To the card: 24 percent is a fire, 4.5 is furniture
To the student loan, since the balance is the larger one
To savings, until there is a cushion behind the payments
quiz.explain: Sort by rate. Toxic-rate debt is the emergency; low-rate debt can even lose to index-fund returns on spare dollars.

quiz.q: "Can you lower my APR?" is…
options: Not worth making, because the rate is set by the contract
A real call that often works for an on-time customer
Worth making only once your credit is close to spotless
Risky, since asking flags the account for review
quiz.explain: Retention is cheaper than acquisition; the person on the phone has options. Two minutes, real success rate, and the ask costs nothing.

cards.back: Every balance, rate, minimum. Ten minutes. Debt strategy is impossible without visibility. The monster shrinks when measured.
24% card = fire. 4.5% student loan = furniture. Sort by rate, not by guilt or size.
Spare dollars at the highest rate first. Mathematically optimal, for spreadsheet people who won't quit.
Spare dollars at the smallest balance first. Wins early, motivation compounds. Optimal for humans.
Engineered to last decades: 20+ years on a typical card balance. The floor that prevents damage, never the plan.
1) "Can you lower my APR?" It works surprisingly often. 2) Balance transfer at 0% intro: a cheat code IF the freed card stays quiet.

debt-strategically.action: Make the one-page list tonight: every balance, rate, and minimum. Sort by rate. Circle the fire, pick avalanche or snowball, and point this month's spare dollars at one target.

emergency-funds.hook: A boring account with three months of rent in it will change your personality.

blocks.text: An emergency fund is insurance you sell to yourself, not an investment. It earns almost nothing, sits in an almost-boring account, and quietly rewires your life: bad bosses become survivable, bad apartments become leavable, and a dead car battery becomes an errand instead of a crisis.
How much, actually

items: Starter: $1,000. This is the "flat tire doesn't hit the credit card" tier. Get here fast, before extra debt payments, before investing beyond the match.
Full: 3 months of bare-bones expenses (rent, food, transport, insurance, minimums), not 3 months of your lifestyle.
Extended: 6 months if your income is variable, you freelance, you're the family's safety net, or your industry does layoff seasons.

blocks.title: Real talk
blocks.text: If your family leans on you, if a parent's emergency becomes your emergency, your fund needs to be bigger than the textbook says, and that's not a flaw in the plan. Budget for the reality you actually have, not the one in the example problems.
Where it lives

A high-yield savings account (HYSA) at an online bank: FDIC-insured, earning real interest, and (this is the feature) one deliberate step away from your checking. Not in stocks (crashes and layoffs carpool), not in crypto, not in your checking account where it will quietly become "money." Separate bank, boring name on the account like "Do Not Touch."

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: Leila, 26, bare-bones month = $2,400. Targets: $1,000 starter (done in 3 months at $340/month), then $7,200 full fund. She automates $300/month to an HYSA the day after payday. Eighteen months later, her company does layoffs. She's calm in every meeting, because she's carrying six months of runway. Same job, different spine.
What counts as an emergency

Job loss, medical bills, urgent travel to family, the car that gets you to work, the laptop your income depends on. Not: sales, weddings (foreseeable; see sinking funds), or vacations. The test: unexpected AND necessary AND urgent. When you do spend from it, that's the fund working, not failing. Refill it first, feel bad never.

blocks.caption: of Americans can't cover a $1,000 emergency from savings. The starter tier alone puts you in the calm half of the country.

quiz.q: The emergency fund's actual job is…
options: Growth, so it should be invested like the rest of it
Insurance you sell yourself: crises become errands
Showing a lender that you can handle a larger loan
The early foundation of what becomes retirement money
quiz.explain: It earns almost nothing and does almost everything: survivable bad bosses, leavable bad apartments, calm layoffs. The return is optionality.

quiz.q: "Three months of expenses" means…
options: Three months of the life you are currently living
Three months of basics: rent, food, transport, bills
Three months of gross salary, before anything comes out
Whatever amount lets you sleep through the night
quiz.explain: Size it on survival mode, not lifestyle mode. That's the number that keeps you alive between jobs, and it's smaller than you feared.

quiz.q: Why keep it in an HYSA instead of index funds?
options: A savings account pays more over a long enough stretch
Layoffs and crashes arrive together; it stays boring
Investing it would tie the money up past the notice period
Lenders want to see the balance sitting in a bank account
quiz.explain: The one time you need this money is exactly when markets are most likely to be down. Insurance can't be volatile.

quiz.q: You spent $800 from the fund on an urgent car repair. This means…
options: The plan did not hold, so the number was set too low
The fund worked. Refill it first and skip the guilt
The card would have been better, keeping the fund whole
It was not really an emergency at under a thousand dollars
quiz.explain: Spending it on unexpected+necessary+urgent is the entire purpose. Refilling becomes the top priority; shame isn't part of the system.

cards.back: $1,000 starter (fast, before extra investing) → 3 months bare-bones → 6 months if income is variable or family leans on you.
Rent + food + transport + insurance + minimums. Size the fund on survival mode, not lifestyle mode.
High-yield savings at a separate online bank. FDIC-insured, real interest, one deliberate step from checking. Name it "Do Not Touch."
Crashes and layoffs carpool. The fund must be boring exactly when everything else isn't.
Unexpected AND necessary AND urgent. Weddings and sales are foreseeable; that's what sinking funds are for.
That's the purpose, not a failure. Refill first, feel bad never.

emergency-funds.action: Open a high-yield savings account this week (15 minutes) and automate the first transfer for the day after payday, even $50. Name the account something that talks back.

negotiation.hook: Rent, bills, salaries: everything is negotiable more often than you think, and the asking voice doesn't have to shake.

blocks.text: Negotiation isn't a personality type reserved for loud people. It's a small set of learnable sentences delivered calmly to another human who usually has more flexibility than their first answer admits. This unit is everyday negotiation; the full salary playbook lives in The 14th Grade.
The three rules that carry every negotiation

items: Ask. The default answer to the unasked question is no. Most people lose negotiations they never started.
Anchor with a number and a reason. "Given X, I was thinking [number]" beats "could you maybe do better?" every time.
Silence after the ask. The gap is uncomfortable on both sides; whoever fills it first concedes something.

blocks.text: Scripts for real life

blocks.title: Copy these
items: Rent renewal: "I've been a reliable tenant for two years, always on time. Comparable units nearby list at $X. Can we keep my renewal at [number]?" Landlords price in turnover costs: an empty month costs them more than your discount.

Bills (internet, phone, insurance): "I'm looking at switching, and [competitor] offers X. Is there a retention rate you can move me to?" Say 'retention'; it routes you to the department with actual discounts.
Medical bills: "I can't pay this in full. Is there a self-pay discount, or an interest-free payment plan?" Hospitals settle and discount constantly; the sticker price is an opening position.
Big purchases: "If we can do [number], I can decide today." Certainty is currency. Trade it for price.

blocks.title: Real talk
blocks.text: If haggling feels shameful, like something respectable people don't do, remember the other side already negotiated: the first rent, the first quote, the sticker price ARE their negotiation moves. Calm asking isn't rude. It's participation.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: Nadia's internet bill creeps to $85. She calls, says the word "retention," cites a competitor's $55 intro offer, and sits through one uncomfortable pause. Result: $58/month for 12 months, which is $324 saved for nine minutes, most of which was hold music. Her rent renewal, same season, same method: listed at +$150, settled at +$50. Two calls, $1,524 a year.
Know your walk-away before you dial

Decide in advance what you'll do if the answer is no: switch providers, accept, escalate, or leave. A negotiation with no walk-away plan is a request for permission. With one, no is just information, and oddly, the calm that comes from having a plan B is exactly what makes plan A say yes more often.

blocks.caption: the typical length of a bill-negotiation call, hold music included. Few hourly rates in your life will ever beat it.

quiz.q: Why does anchoring with a number and a reason beat "can you do better?"
options: It signals that you have done the background research
It gives them something concrete, and sets the range
It comes across as more polite than an open question
A stated figure is harder for them to walk back later
quiz.explain: Vague asks get vague discounts. A reasoned number frames the negotiation around YOUR figure instead of theirs.

quiz.q: The magic word when calling about a bill is…
options: Discount, which is the outcome you are actually after
Manager, since authority sits a level above the front line
Retention: the desk that exists to stop you leaving
Cancel, which forces the system to make you an offer
quiz.explain: Front-line support can't do much; retention exists to stop you leaving and has real offers. Name the department and you skip a level.

quiz.q: Why decide your walk-away before the conversation?
options: So you can put it on the table if the talk stalls out
Without one you ask permission; with one, no is data
Because a stated limit is what makes an offer binding
So the conversation finishes inside a sensible window
quiz.explain: A plan B changes your posture more than your words. The other side can hear whether you have options.

quiz.q: "Haggling is embarrassing." The reframe:
options: It is, a little, so save it for salary and rent alone
The sticker price was their move; asking is participation
Do it in writing, where nobody has to feel the awkwardness
The discomfort is a signal that the ask is out of line
quiz.explain: The negotiation started before you arrived; declining to participate just means accepting their opening offer.

cards.back: Ask (unasked = automatic no) · Anchor with number + reason · Silence after the ask.
"Reliable tenant, always on time, comparables at $X. Can we keep renewal at [number]?" Empty months cost landlords more than your discount.
Say "retention" on bill calls; it routes you to the department with real discounts. Cite one competitor offer.
Sticker price is an opening position. Ask for the self-pay discount or an interest-free plan; hospitals settle constantly.
"If we can do [number], I can decide today." Trade your decisiveness for their price.
Decide what you'll do on a no before you dial. Without it you're asking permission; with it, no is information.

negotiation.action: Pick your ugliest recurring bill and make the retention call this week: competitor offer cited, one number anchored, one silence survived. Report the savings to someone.

the-big-calls.hook: Big decisions feel heavy because you're trying to be certain. You don't need certain. You need a process.

blocks.text: Take the job or stay? Move cities? Get serious or step back? School teaches you to find THE right answer. Life's big calls don't have one. They have trade-offs, deadlines, and incomplete information. So the skill is deciding well, not being right.
Reversible vs irreversible: sort first

Most decisions are two-way doors: you can walk through, look around, and walk back. Taking a job is more reversible than it feels: you can leave. Moving cities is reversible. A few are one-way doors: having kids, burning a relationship on the way out, certain debts. The rule: move fast through two-way doors, slow down hard for one-way doors. Most people do the opposite: agonizing over reversible calls and sleepwalking into permanent ones.

blocks.title: Real talk
blocks.text: "What if I make the wrong choice?" For a reversible decision, the wrong choice costs you a detour. Staying frozen costs you the year. Indecision is also a decision, just with worse terms.
Three lenses that catch what you'd miss

items: 10/10/10: how will I feel about this in 10 minutes, 10 months, 10 years? Fear lives in the 10-minute view; your actual life lives in the 10-year view.
The friend test: if my best friend described this exact situation, what would I tell them? You already know. You're just afraid to say it to yourself.
Expected downside: what's the realistic worst case, and can I recover from it? If yes, the fear is mostly noise.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: Dev has a stable job and an offer at a smaller company: more scope, less brand name. Sort: reversible (a two-way door; he can job-hunt again). 10/10/10: nervous now, likely proud in 10 months, and in 10 years the "safe" logo won't matter. Friend test: he'd tell a friend to go. Worst case: the startup struggles and he job-hunts in 18 months with more experience. Recoverable. He goes. Not because it's guaranteed, but because the process says the downside is survivable and the upside compounds.
Deciding with other people in the room

Real calls involve parents, partners, money, and expectations. Two things help. First, separate the decision from the announcement: figure out what you actually think before you manage everyone's reactions. Second, when family pressure is part of the equation, name the real trade-off out loud: "this path costs me X, that one costs them Y." It turns a guilt fog into a conversation with terms.

blocks.caption: of the information is usually enough. Waiting for 90% certainty on a reversible call mostly just means someone else got there first, or the window closed.

quiz.q: First move on any big decision?
options: Lay every possible outcome out where you can weigh them
Sort it: is this a two-way door, or a one-way door?
Ask five people you trust and look for the pattern
Give it a month, because time reveals what you want
quiz.explain: The sort decides the speed. Reversible calls deserve fast, decent decisions; irreversible ones deserve the slow, careful treatment. Most people reverse this.

quiz.q: The 10/10/10 lens asks…
options: For ten pros, ten cons, and ten alternatives on paper
How this will feel in 10 minutes, 10 months, 10 years
Whether ten people you respect would agree with it
Whether it costs more than 10, 100 or 1,000 dollars
quiz.explain: Fear dominates the 10-minute view. The 10-year view is where your actual life happens; the lens exists to get you out of the short-term panic frame.

quiz.q: Why does the friend test work?
options: Someone outside the situation can see it more clearly
It takes your fear out; you knew and would not say it
It shares the responsibility if the call turns out badly
It does not: advice you give yourself is the least trusted
quiz.explain: Describing your situation as someone else's strips the fear and self-image out. What's left is usually the answer you've been avoiding.

quiz.q: You have 70% of the information on a reversible call. The move is…
options: Hold out for 90: a big call deserves full information
Decide: certainty costs more than a recoverable miss
Pick at random, because the remaining 30 is unknowable
Pass it to somebody who has made this call before
quiz.explain: On reversible decisions, the cost of frozen months usually beats the cost of a correctable mistake. Certainty is for one-way doors.

cards.back: A reversible decision: you can walk through and walk back. Move fast on these. Most decisions are this kind, even when they feel permanent.
An irreversible decision: kids, burned bridges, certain debts. These are the ones that deserve the slow, careful treatment.
How will I feel in 10 minutes / 10 months / 10 years? Fear lives in the first frame; your life lives in the last one.
If your best friend described this exact situation, what would you tell them? You already know. Say it to yourself.
Define the realistic worst case and ask: can I recover? If yes, most of the remaining fear is noise.
On reversible calls, deciding at ~70% of the information beats waiting for certainty. Indecision has a price too; it's just quieter.

the-big-calls.action: Write down one real decision you've been circling. Sort it (two-way or one-way door), run 10/10/10 and the friend test on paper, and give yourself a decision deadline: date and time.

first-apartments.hook: The lease is a contract someone wrote to win. Read it like they meant it.

blocks.text: Your first apartment is three decisions wearing one trench coat: a financial decision (the biggest line in your budget), a legal decision (a binding contract), and a lifestyle decision (roommates, commute, sleep). Most people make it in a weekend under pressure. Here's the slow-down.
The real monthly number

Rent is the headline; the real number is rent + utilities + internet + renter's insurance (~$15/month, not optional in practice) + parking or transit + the amortized move itself (deposit, first/last, truck, furniture). A $1,400 apartment is routinely a $1,750 life. The classic guardrail says keep rent around 30% of take-home; in expensive cities that may be aspirational; then the guardrail becomes: know exactly what the overage is costing your other goals.

blocks.title: Before you sign: the walkthrough checklist
items: Water pressure and hot water: run the shower, actually.
Every window and lock. Cell signal in every room.
Photos of EVERY existing scuff and stain, timestamped, emailed to the landlord. This is your deposit's bodyguard.
Visit at night. The street at 10pm is a different street.
Read the lease for: guest policy, sublet rules, rent-increase terms, early-exit penalty, who fixes what, and exactly how you get the deposit back.

blocks.title: Real talk
blocks.text: The deposit games are where first-timers lose money. Your protections are boring and powerful: the timestamped photo email on day one, a written move-out inspection, and knowing your state's deadline for deposit returns. Paper beats memory.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: Kiran finds a $1,450 place. Real number: $1,450 + $130 utilities + $60 internet + $15 insurance + $90 parking = $1,745, which is 36% of take-home. The alternative with a roommate: $1,050 all-in, 22%. He runs the difference: $8,300 a year, a fully-funded emergency fund plus a vacation, for the price of sharing a kitchen for one more year. He takes the roommate on purpose, with a number attached, not as a defeat.
Roommates: the pre-nup conversation

Money 101 says every dollar needs a job; roommate harmony says every scenario needs an agreement BEFORE move-in: how rent splits (equal, or by room size?), how utilities get paid and by whom, guest limits, quiet hours, groceries, and (the big one) what happens if someone needs to leave early. One awkward hour before the lease beats twelve resentful months after.

blocks.caption: of take-home pay: the classic rent guardrail. Break it knowingly if you must, but know exactly which other goal is paying for the view.

quiz.q: The "real monthly number" for a $1,400 apartment is…
options: $1,400, which is the figure you agreed to pay monthly
Rent plus utilities, internet, insurance and parking
$1,400 plus the deposit, spread over the first year
Whatever the listing quotes once fees are included
quiz.explain: Budget on the all-in number. The $1,400 headline is routinely a $1,750 life, and the surprise is where budgets die.

quiz.q: The single best protector of your security deposit:
options: A good relationship with the landlord from day one
Dated photos of every flaw, emailed on day one
A clean payment record across the whole of the lease
A walkthrough together before you hand the keys back
quiz.explain: Paper beats memory, and email creates a record with a date. The day-one photo email is your deposit's bodyguard at move-out.

quiz.q: Why visit the apartment at night before signing?
options: An evening viewing gets you more of the agent's time
The street at 10pm is a different street entirely
Evening is when the neighbours are actually home to meet
Landlords price more flexibly outside of office hours
quiz.explain: You're leasing the location at all hours, not just the sunny Saturday showing.

quiz.q: The roommate conversation that matters most BEFORE move-in:
options: Whose furniture goes where, so the place works day one
Rent split, bills, guests, and who covers an early exit
How you will handle it if one of you starts dating someone
Nothing: raising money with friends sours the whole thing
quiz.explain: The early-exit scenario is the one that torches friendships. One awkward hour before beats twelve resentful months after.

cards.back: Rent + utilities + internet + renter's insurance + parking/transit + amortized move-in. A $1,400 listing is a ~$1,750 life.
Rent near 30% of take-home. Breakable in expensive cities, but know which goal is paying the difference.
Day one: timestamped photos of every flaw, emailed to the landlord. Move-out: written inspection. Paper beats memory.
Guest policy, sublets, rent-increase terms, early-exit penalty, repairs, deposit-return process. Read for these six.
The street at 10pm is a different street. Lease the location at all hours.
Splits, bills, guests, quiet hours, and the early-exit plan, agreed BEFORE the lease, in writing, while everyone's friends.

first-apartments.action: Moving soon or not, compute your real monthly housing number today: current place or target place, all-in. Check it against 30% of take-home and see what the gap is funding or costing.

career-moves.hook: Your career is a portfolio of skills and stories, and every year adds an asset or repeats one.

blocks.text: Nobody owes you a career path anymore; the ladder got replaced by a climbing wall. That's scarier and better: moves in any direction, but you have to choose the holds. The skill of this unit is reading your own situation clearly, a lighter companion to the full quit-or-stay framework in The 15th Grade.
The yearly audit: four questions

items: Learning: did the last 12 months teach me more than the 12 before? Flat learning is slow-motion falling behind.
Earning: has my pay kept pace with what my role earns on the open market? (Check listings for your title yearly; takes an hour.)
Story: can I describe this year as a chapter with results ("built X, grew Y, fixed Z") or just as attendance?
Energy: does the work mostly fill or mostly drain? Not every week; the trend line.

blocks.text: Score honestly. Four greens: stay and push deeper. Two or more reds for two audits in a row: the wall is telling you to look at other holds.

blocks.title: Real talk
blocks.text: Loyalty is a virtue between people, not between you and a payroll system. Companies conduct their own yearly audit of you; it's called a compensation review. Auditing back is symmetrical, not disloyal.
Moves that aren't quitting

The audit failing doesn't only mean "leave." Internal moves are underrated: a transfer to a growing team, a scope expansion ("I want to own X. What would it take?"), a manager change, a skills budget. Companies would usually rather re-pot you than lose you, but only if you ask. The chapter on asking is called Negotiation, and you've read it.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: Tara's audit, year 3: learning red (nothing new since year 1), earning red (listings pay $15k more), story yellow, energy yellow. Instead of rage-quitting, she runs the sequence: asks for scope (gets a maybe), interviews externally anyway, lands an offer at +$18k, brings it home once, without theatrics. Company matches at +$14k with a new team. She takes the match, and the audit next year is four greens. The offer was information everyone needed, not a threat.
Always be two moves deep

The best career insurance is quiet and continuous: a resume updated every six months while memories are fresh, a network fed BEFORE it's needed (two coffees a quarter with people you actually like), and one skill compounding at three hours a week. People with options negotiate differently, get treated differently, and, strangely, end up needing the options less.

blocks.caption: a year, checking what your title pays on the open market. Compensation drift is silent; the market check is the smoke alarm.

quiz.q: The four yearly audit questions:
options: Salary, job title, where you sit, and who you report to
Learning, earning, the story it tells, and your energy
Promotion timing, bonus, vacation days, and equity
Your age, tenure, the industry, and what you studied
quiz.explain: Growth, market pay, a describable chapter, and the fill/drain trend line. Two+ reds twice in a row = look at other holds.

quiz.q: "Auditing" your employer yearly is…
options: Disloyal, if they have been good to you so far
Symmetrical: they run one on you every review cycle
A thing to do only once you are already unhappy there
Risky, since that kind of thinking tends to show
quiz.explain: Loyalty is between people. The company already measures your value annually; measuring back is just being awake.

quiz.q: The audit fails but you like the company. First moves:
options: Leave anyway: a failed audit is a failed audit
Ask internally: scope, transfer, manager, skills budget
Give it another year and see whether it corrects itself
Take it to HR, who are paid to resolve exactly this
quiz.explain: "I want to own X. What would it take?" opens doors resignation letters close. Leaving is one move among several.

quiz.q: Why update your resume every six months even when happy?
options: It keeps you visible to recruiters watching the market
Results fade fast, and options change how you ask
Most employers expect a current one on file internally
It is a useful ritual for noticing how far you have come
quiz.explain: The best career insurance is maintained while things are fine: fresh resume, fed network, one compounding skill. Options change posture.

cards.back: Learning · Earning · Story · Energy. Two+ reds, two audits running = the wall is talking.
One hour a year reading listings for your title. Compensation drift is silent; this is the smoke alarm.
Can you describe the year as "built X, grew Y, fixed Z", or only as attendance? Chapters, not tenure.
Scope expansion, team transfer, manager change, skills budget. Companies re-pot people who ask.
Resume refreshed every 6 months, two coffees a quarter, one skill at 3 hrs/week. Insurance is built while employed.
A virtue between people, not between you and a payroll system that audits you annually.

career-moves.action: Run the four-question audit on paper for your current (or most recent) year, and do the one-hour market check on your title. Two numbers and four colors: that's your career dashboard.

new-cities.hook: Moving cities is buying a new life with two currencies: money and loneliness. Budget for both.

blocks.text: A new city can be the highest-return decision available to a young person: new market, new pay scale, new self. It can also be an expensive way to be sad somewhere with better weather. The difference is rarely the city; it's whether you ran the two budgets before the truck came.
Budget one: the money

items: Cost-of-living is a ratio, not a vibe: same salary in a city where rent doubles is a pay cut wearing a skyline.
The move itself: truck or flights, deposits stacking on deposits, first furniture, overlap month of double rent. Realistic range: $3–8k. Have it in cash before you commit.
The runway rule: land with 3 months of the NEW city's expenses, minimum, or 6 if you're arriving without a job.
Taxes and quirks: state income tax varies from 0% to 13%+; car insurance, parking, and broker fees change city math more than lattes do.

blocks.text: Budget two: the loneliness

The unglamorous truth: months 2 through 6 are the valley. The novelty wears off before the friendships wear in, and friendships at adult speed need repetition, not chemistry. The fix is structural: two recurring commitments (a league, a class, a volunteer shift, a faith community; anything weekly with the same humans) booked in month one, BEFORE you feel like it. Motivation follows attendance.

blocks.title: Real talk
blocks.text: If moving means leaving parents who depend on you (for care, for translation, for Sunday dinners), that's a real cost, not sentimentality, and it belongs in the decision on paper. Sometimes the answer is a city two hours away instead of a coast away. Distance has settings.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: Rohan weighs Austin (+$14k salary) against staying in Jersey near family. The math: Austin's rent +$400/month, no state income tax +$260/month, flights home ~$2,000/year. Net: roughly +$6k, real but not life-changing. The deciding factors turn out to be non-financial: a two-hour time difference for his mom's calls, and that his industry's center of gravity is in Austin. He goes, with six months' runway, two leagues joined by week three, and a promise of four trips home a year, budgeted.
The trial and the exit

Before signing a year anywhere: spend a working week there if you can: commute at rush hour, grocery-shop, sit in the neighborhood at 9pm. And set a review date, not a life sentence: "eighteen months, then I decide again with data." Moves are two-way doors; treating them as reversible is what makes them brave instead of reckless.

blocks.caption: the valley months, when novelty has faded and friendships haven't formed. Book the recurring commitments in month one; attendance beats motivation.

quiz.q: A +$14k offer in a city where rent is +$700/month is…
options: A fourteen thousand dollar raise, before tax is taken
Break-even: rent is the biggest term in the ratio
Worth taking regardless, for what the move teaches you
A worse deal, since bigger cities tax you on everything
quiz.explain: $8,400 of the raise is spoken for by rent alone before taxes and quirks. Run the ratio, then decide; sometimes the non-financial factors are the real deciders.

quiz.q: The runway rule for landing in a new city:
options: One month of expenses, so the first rent is covered
Three months of the new city, or six with no job yet
Nothing extra, provided the job offer is already signed
Enough set aside to get yourself home if it goes wrong
quiz.explain: Deposits stack, jobs wobble, cars break. Runway is what makes the first bad month a story instead of a spiral.

quiz.q: The loneliness budget is best spent on…
options: A better apartment, since you will be in it a lot
Two weekly commitments with the same people, booked early
Regular trips home, which keep the real friendships alive
Time with colleagues, who become the easiest friends to make
quiz.explain: Adult friendship runs on repetition, not chemistry. Structure beats motivation, especially in the month-2-to-6 valley.

quiz.q: Leaving parents who rely on you is…
options: Sentiment, and it does not belong in a real decision
A cost that belongs on paper; distance has settings
A reason to stay, whatever else the move would offer
Worth weighing only if they say something about it
quiz.explain: Care, translation, presence: real line items. Naming them honestly sometimes lands on a two-hour city instead of a coast, and that can be the optimal answer.

cards.back: Money (ratio, move costs, runway, taxes) and loneliness (the month 2–6 valley). Both need funding before the truck.
Same salary, doubled rent = a pay cut wearing a skyline. Run new-city expenses against new-city pay.
Land with 3 months of the new city's expenses, or 6 without a job. Deposits stack; runway absorbs the wobble.
Months 2–6: novelty gone, friendships not yet formed. Everyone gets it; structure is the way through.
Two weekly commitments with the same humans, booked in month one. Adult friendship is an attendance sport.
"18 months, then I decide again with data." Moves are two-way doors; reversibility is what makes them brave.

new-cities.action: Pick a city you've wondered about and run budget one on paper tonight: real listings, tax difference, move cost, runway number. Even if you never go, now the daydream has a price tag.

big-relationships.hook: You'll interview harder for a job than most people do for a life partner. Fix the ratio.

blocks.text: Choosing a partner is the biggest financial, emotional, and logistical decision most people ever make. It just doesn't feel like a decision because it arrives disguised as a feeling. The feeling matters. It's also not the whole interview. This unit is the intro; the money-specific conversations get their own full unit in The 15th Grade.
What actually predicts "works"

items: How you fight, not whether: contempt (eye-rolling, mockery) is the strongest divorce predictor researchers have found. Disagreement is weather; contempt is climate.
Repair speed: how fast after a fight does someone reach across? Hours vs weeks is a compatibility metric.
Direction match: kids or not, city or suburb, faith, ambition level, how family fits. Chemistry doesn't resolve destination conflicts; it postpones them.
Admiration that survives Tuesday: do you still respect who they are when nothing exciting is happening?

blocks.title: Real talk
blocks.text: Where families are involved in matches (introductions, opinions, expectations), the framework still holds. A family's approval is a data point, sometimes a wise one; the direction-match and how-you-fight questions are still yours to run. Nobody else attends the marriage.
The conversations that decide everything

Moving in, marriage, kids: each is a one-way-door-ish call that deserves actual words, not drift. The pattern that fails: sliding (lease is up anyway, wedding because it's been three years) instead of deciding. Couples who DECIDE at each threshold, out loud, with the direction questions on the table, consistently report stronger outcomes than couples who slid. The talk is the commitment; the party is just the announcement.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: Sana and Omar, two years in, lease ending. Sliding version: move in, save rent, see what happens. Deciding version: one dinner, four questions: are we pointing at marriage or testing it? Whose career leads if they conflict? Kids someday, and roughly when? What does 'supporting our parents' mean to each of us? Two questions match, one needs work, one they'd never said out loud. They still move in, but as a decision with a direction, not a drift with a discount.
Red flags vs rough edges

Rough edges: different tidiness standards, hobbies you don't share, awkward with your friends at first. Workable; that's what systems and time are for. Red flags: contempt as a habit, control (money, clothes, friends, location), secrets with structure (hidden accounts, hidden relationships), and anyone you're afraid to disagree with. Rough edges get sanded; red flags get bigger with commitment. The difference decides whether to invest the next year or spend it leaving well.

blocks.caption: contempt: the single strongest predictor of relationship failure in decades of research. Watch how someone disagrees with you; it's the trailer for the marriage.

quiz.q: The strongest researched predictor of relationship failure:
options: Money: mismatched habits around it wear a couple down
Contempt: mockery and eye-rolling as a habit
Sharing none of the same interests or weekend plans
Distance, and the years it can quietly stretch to
quiz.explain: Disagreement is weather; contempt is climate. How someone fights with you is the trailer for the whole film.

quiz.q: "Sliding vs deciding" refers to…
options: How quickly people move between apps and matches
Drifting into thresholds instead of choosing them
Whether the physical side of it came early or later
Which person raises the question of getting married
quiz.explain: The lease being up is not a reason to merge lives. The talk is the commitment; the party is the announcement.

quiz.q: Which is a rough edge rather than a red flag?
options: You find yourself afraid to disagree with them
They have opinions about who you see and what you spend
Different standards of tidiness, and separate hobbies
There are accounts and messages you are not shown
quiz.explain: Rough edges respond to systems and time. Control, structured secrets, and fear grow WITH commitment; they don't sand down.

quiz.q: Family involvement in choosing a partner means the framework…
options: Does not really apply, since the choice is a shared one
Still applies: approval is input, the core checks are yours
Is replaced by the judgment of people with more experience
Matters mostly later, once the marriage is actually underway
quiz.explain: Family wisdom can be real input. But nobody else attends the marriage; the core questions stay yours.

cards.back: How you fight (contempt = climate) · repair speed · direction match · admiration that survives Tuesday.
Drifting through thresholds vs deciding out loud at each one. Deciders do better; the talk IS the commitment.
Pointing at marriage or testing? Whose career leads in conflict? Kids, roughly when? What does supporting parents mean to each of us?
Edges (tidiness, hobbies) sand down with time. Flags (contempt, control, structured secrets, fear of disagreeing) grow with commitment.
How fast someone reaches across after a fight (hours vs weeks) is a compatibility metric, not a personality quirk.
The #1 researched predictor of failure. Watch how they disagree with you: it's the trailer for the marriage.

big-relationships.action: Partnered or still evaluating, write the four threshold questions somewhere private and answer them for yourself first. You can't compare answers you haven't formed.

health-insurance.hook: You don't need to love health insurance. You need to stop being afraid of five words.

blocks.text: Health insurance is deliberately confusing, and confusion is expensive: people skip care they've already paid for, or get ambushed by bills they could have routed around. Five terms, one worked example, and the fear mostly dissolves.

blocks.title: The five words
items: Premium: the monthly subscription. You pay it no matter what.
Deductible: what you pay out of pocket each year BEFORE insurance starts sharing costs.
Copay: the flat fee per visit or prescription ($25 to see a doctor), often available before the deductible is met.
Coinsurance: the split after the deductible, like 20% you / 80% them.
Out-of-pocket maximum: the yearly ceiling on YOUR total spending. Past this, insurance pays 100%. This number is the whole reason insurance exists: it's where bankruptcy protection lives.

blocks.text: One bill, walked through

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: Maya's plan: $2,000 deductible, 20% coinsurance, $6,500 out-of-pocket max. An ER visit bills $9,000. She pays the remaining $1,400 of her deductible, then 20% of the next chunk until her payments total $6,500; insurance covers everything past that ceiling. Painful, capped, survivable, and exactly the math her emergency fund was sized for. Without insurance, the bill is the full $9,000 plus sticker-price markups.
The network is the trap door

In-network means negotiated prices; out-of-network can mean full freight, sometimes barely covered. The two-minute habit that saves four figures: before any planned visit, check "is this provider in-network for MY plan": the doctor, the facility, AND (for procedures) the anesthesiologist. Federal surprise-billing rules now protect you in emergencies and for out-of-network providers at in-network facilities, but planned care is still on you to route.

blocks.title: Real talk
blocks.text: Skipping the doctor to save money while insured is usually backwards: preventive visits (annual physical, vaccines, screenings) are typically covered at 100% before the deductible. You already paid for them via premiums. Going is the frugal move.
No employer plan?

Under 26: a parent's plan is usually the cheapest ticket, even if you live elsewhere. Otherwise: healthcare.gov marketplace plans with income-based subsidies (most young buyers qualify for real discounts), or Medicaid if income is low; no shame, that's what it's for. The uninsured "strategy" is a lottery ticket where the prize is bankruptcy: one appendix, one accident, one diagnosis.

blocks.caption: what most plans pay for preventive care (physicals, vaccines, screenings), even before the deductible. You already bought it. Use it.

quiz.q: The out-of-pocket maximum is…
options: The most the insurer will pay out in a single year
The yearly cap on your spending; then they cover it
Another name for the deductible, worded differently
A headline figure that rarely applies to a real claim
quiz.explain: Premiums buy you a worst-case ceiling. Know this number and size your emergency fund with it in mind.

quiz.q: You're insured with a $2,000 deductible you haven't touched. A $150 doctor visit costs you…
options: Nothing at all, because the coverage is already active
The negotiated rate, or a copay: the deductible first
The full two thousand, since that is what you owe first
A fifth of it, with the insurer covering the remainder
quiz.explain: Before the deductible you pay most costs at the plan's negotiated rates; copays are the common exception. Insurance sharing starts after the deductible.

quiz.q: The two-minute habit before planned procedures:
options: Ask the doctor whether this one tends to be expensive
Check the facility and anesthetist are in network
Have a way to pay on the day, so nothing gets delayed
Book it early in the year, before the deductible resets
quiz.explain: Out-of-network is the trap door. Surprise-billing rules protect emergencies, but planned care is yours to route in-network.

quiz.q: Skipping your annual physical to save money is…
options: Sensible, given how little a healthy year turns up
Backwards: preventive care is usually free
Reasonable while you are young and feeling fine
A choice you only really have on certain plans
quiz.explain: Preventive visits are usually free before the deductible, and they catch expensive things while they're cheap things.

cards.back: Premium (monthly) · deductible (you-first threshold) · copay (flat visit fee) · coinsurance (the split after) · out-of-pocket max (your yearly ceiling).
The whole point of insurance: a ceiling on your worst year. Past it, they pay 100%. Size your emergency fund with it in mind.
Before planned care: provider, facility, AND anesthesiologist in-network for YOUR plan. Two minutes, four figures.
Physicals, vaccines, screenings: typically 100% covered before the deductible. Already paid for. Go.
A parent's plan is usually the cheapest coverage, even living in another city. After that: marketplace subsidies or Medicaid.
A lottery ticket where the prize is bankruptcy. One appendix, one accident. The marketplace subsidy probably costs less than your phone plan.

health-insurance.action: Find your plan's five numbers this week (insurance app or HR portal): premium, deductible, copay, coinsurance, out-of-pocket max. Write them where future-you can find them in a waiting room.

family-money-talks.hook: Money flows through families in every direction. The ones that stay healthy talk about it out loud.

blocks.text: Maybe you're the first in your family to earn like this. Maybe parents helped you and it's time to help back. Maybe help is expected monthly, assumed, unspoken. Family money is the least-taught subject in this course because every family treats it as private, which is exactly why the patterns repeat.
Helping parents without sinking yourself

The instinct says give whatever's asked; the math says a drowning lifeguard saves no one. The sustainable version is a NUMBER: a line in your budget like rent, decided in calm, not negotiated fresh during each crisis. "I can do $400 a month, every month, reliably" beats sporadic $1,500 rescues that wreck your savings and still feel like never enough. Reliability is worth more to your parents than heroics; a number is worth more to you than a fog.

blocks.title: Real talk
blocks.text: In many immigrant families, supporting parents is the repayment of a sacrifice you watched happen, not a choice. This unit doesn't argue with that. It argues for doing it ON PURPOSE: a number, a schedule, and your own oxygen mask (emergency fund, retirement match) still on first. Guilt-driven giving collapses; planned giving compounds.
Money flowing the other way

blocks.title: Taking help without strings tangling
items: Name the terms out loud: gift or loan? If loan: amount, schedule, and what happens if you're late. Write it down; paper protects love.
Understand what accepting costs: help sometimes arrives bundled with a vote on your choices. Decide if the bundle is worth it BEFORE accepting.
A gift with a thank-you beats a loan with a fog. Fog is where resentment grows on both sides.

blocks.text: Lending to family (and the sibling question)

The oldest rule is still the best: lend only what you can afford to lose, and consider it mentally spent the moment it leaves. If it comes back, wonderful. If it can't be lost, say no with an alternative ("I can't lend that, but I can help with X"). And when siblings share the parent-support load unevenly: one honest conversation about who-does-what (money, time, logistics; all three count as contribution) beats a decade of silent scorekeeping at every holiday.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: Anh, 27, sends her parents money "whenever they need it", which is unpredictably, painfully, and always at the worst time. New system, one dinner: $350 monthly, automated, plus a $1,000 yearly buffer for surprises, agreed with her brother who covers the parents' phone plan and drives them to appointments (his contribution counted out loud, in front of everyone). Her savings rate recovers; her mother stops apologizing when she calls; her brother stops feeling invisible. Same love, with a structure under it.

blocks.caption: a reliable monthly figure, decided in calm: the thing that beats sporadic heroics for your parents AND your savings rate. Fog is the enemy; the number is the fix.

quiz.q: The sustainable structure for supporting parents:
options: Give what is asked, whenever the asking happens
A budgeted number, decided calmly, after your own basics
Nothing at all until your own position is genuinely secure
Larger amounts at holidays, when it is most useful to them
quiz.explain: The oxygen-mask rule isn't selfishness: a financially drowning helper eventually helps no one. Reliability beats heroics in both directions.

quiz.q: Accepting a large money gift from parents. The key move:
options: Take it graciously and let the terms stay unspoken
Say it out loud: gift or loan, and if loan, in writing
Decline it, because the strings always turn up eventually
Accept it only as cash, so no record follows it around
quiz.explain: Fog is where resentment grows. Paper protects love; unspoken terms get renegotiated at every family dinner forever.

quiz.q: The rule for lending to family:
options: Never lend to family, whatever the circumstances are
Lend only what you can lose, and count it gone
Charge interest, so that it is treated as a real loan
Lend freely: family is the one place it comes back
quiz.explain: If it comes back, wonderful. If you can't afford to lose it, the answer is a no with an alternative, which protects the relationship better than a resented yes.

quiz.q: Siblings splitting parent support unevenly. The fix:
options: The highest earner covers it and says nothing about it
One honest talk that counts money, time and logistics
An even split, whatever anyone earns or lives near
Let the parents decide who should be contributing what
quiz.explain: Driving to appointments and managing paperwork are contributions. Counting everything out loud once beats silent scorekeeping at a decade of holidays.

cards.back: A reliable monthly figure decided in calm, budgeted like rent, beats sporadic crisis rescues for everyone involved.
Emergency fund and retirement match stay funded while you help. A drowning lifeguard saves no one.
Name terms out loud, write them down. A gift with a thank-you beats a loan with a fog.
Family help sometimes arrives with a vote on your choices attached. Price the bundle before accepting it.
Only what you can afford to lose; mentally spent when it leaves. Otherwise: no + alternative.
Money, time, logistics: all count. One out-loud conversation beats silent scorekeeping forever.

family-money-talks.action: If money flows between you and family in any direction: write the current reality down (amounts, frequency, terms, or the fog where terms should be), and pick ONE conversation from this unit to have this month.

ten-year-view.hook: You massively overestimate what a year changes, and massively underestimate what ten will.

blocks.text: The last unit of The 13th Grade zooms all the way out. Almost everything this course taught (habits, index funds, credit age, skills, relationships) shares one engine: compounding. Small rates, long runways, absurd endings. The ten-year view is the discipline of making today's choices while looking at that runway instead of at this week.
What compounds (and what doesn't)

items: Compounds: invested money, skills that stack, reputation, health habits, relationships tended, an audience or body of work, credit history.
Doesn't: stuff. Most purchases depreciate; most experiences appreciate in memory but don't stack.
Compounds negatively: high-interest debt, avoided conversations, skipped checkups, a network never fed, resentment.
The ten-year question for any recurring choice: is this compounding for me, against me, or not at all?

blocks.title: Real talk
blocks.text: Ten years feels abstract until you do it backwards: ten years ago you were (roughly) in ninth grade or your first job, and it feels like four Tuesdays ago. The next ten will move at the same speed. The person arriving is being assembled by this month's defaults.
Decisions that echo vs decisions that don't

Most of what stresses you this week (the awkward email, the party you skipped, the phone you chose) is noise at the ten-year resolution. A tiny set of choices actually echoes: what you practice daily, who you spend your evenings with, where you live, what you drive INTO debt for, whether the 401(k) box got checked at 24. The skill is spending your worry on the echoing set. Most people budget their anxiety exactly backwards.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: Two friends, both 24, both earning $58k. Dana: checks the 401(k) match box, $250/month to index funds, three hours a week on a skill, calls one friend a week on the commute. Sam: none of that, but a nicer car ($480/month) and a better phone. Neither feels different at 25. At 34: Dana has ~$70k invested, a senior title from the compounded skill, and the friendships that survive everyone's busy decade. Sam has a used car worth $6k and a drawer of old phones. Nobody made a big decision. The decade was decided by defaults.
The graduation assignment

Write the one-page letter: "It's ten years from today. Here's where I live, what I do with a Tuesday, who's around the table, what the accounts look like." Not goals. A scene. Then reverse-engineer ONE default per domain (money, skill, health, people) that the scene requires, and install it this month. That's the whole course in one exercise: the big calls are made of small defaults, chosen on purpose. Class dismissed. The 14th Grade is waiting.

blocks.caption: the runway on which boring monthly defaults become an unrecognizable life, in whichever direction they were pointed.

quiz.q: The core insight of the ten-year view:
options: A decade is long enough to be worth planning in detail
People overrate one year and underrate a decade
Thinking that far ahead costs you the years in between
Ten years out is too uncertain to plan against usefully
quiz.explain: Small rates on long runways produce absurd endings. The year feels slow; the decade moves like four Tuesdays.

quiz.q: Which list is "compounds FOR you"?
options: Cars, phones and furniture, which hold some value
Invested money, skills, reputation, relationships
Collectibles and anything with a scarce supply behind it
Anything expensive enough to still be worth something
quiz.explain: The compounding set stacks on itself. Stuff depreciates; debt and avoided conversations compound against you.

quiz.q: Most people budget their anxiety backwards, meaning…
options: They worry less than the situation actually warrants
They spend it on this week, not the choices that echo
Worrying does no useful work in any of these cases
They should spread the worry evenly across everything
quiz.explain: A tiny set of choices echoes at ten-year resolution. Spend the worry there; the rest is noise that feels loud up close.

quiz.q: The graduation assignment is…
options: A list of the goals you want to have hit in ten years
One page describing an ordinary day, then a default each
A board of images of the life you are aiming yourself at
A five-year plan, revisited and revised once every year
quiz.explain: A scene beats goals because it forces specifics, and defaults beat resolutions because they run without you. Big calls are made of small defaults.

cards.back: One year changes less than you hope; ten change more than you can picture. Compounding needs runway.
Invested money, stacking skills, reputation, health habits, tended relationships, credit history, a body of work.
High-interest debt, avoided conversations, skipped checkups, an unfed network, resentment.
Daily practice, evening company, where you live, debt-financed purchases, the checked 401(k) box. Spend your worry here.
Nobody makes one big decision to have a great or mediocre decade. The monthly defaults do it quietly, either way.
One page: an ordinary Tuesday, ten years out (place, work, people, accounts). Then install one default per domain that the scene requires.

ten-year-view.action: Write the ten-year letter tonight: one page, an ordinary Tuesday, specific. Then install one default it requires (an automation, a weekly block, a standing call) before the week ends.

salary-negotiation.hook: The scariest 30 seconds of your career are worth more than most years of work.

blocks.text: Here's the math nobody shows you: raises compound. A $10,000 higher starting salary, with normal percentage raises on top, is easily $100,000+ over a decade, from one conversation you were too polite to have.
Why negotiating doesn't blow up the offer

The fear is that asking will make the offer disappear. In practice, companies expect it: recruiters have a range, and the first number is almost never the top of it. A respectful ask doesn't read as greedy; it reads as someone who knows how this works. Offers get pulled over rudeness and dishonesty, not over a polite counter.

blocks.title: Real talk
blocks.text: If negotiating feels disrespectful, especially if you were raised to be grateful and not make noise, reframe it: the company negotiated. Their first number was a negotiation move. You're not starting the game, you're just finally playing it.
The script

blocks.title: Four sentences, in order
items: Enthusiasm first: "I'm really excited about this role and the team."
The anchor: "Based on the scope and what I'm seeing for this kind of role, I was expecting something closer to [number 10–15% above their offer]."
One supporting reason: the strongest thing you bring: a skill, a result, a competing signal.
Then silence. The silence is the negotiation. Whoever fills it first, loses ground. Let it sit.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: Anika gets offered $85,000. She says the four sentences with $97,000 as her number, then stops talking. The recruiter comes back at $92,000 plus a $5,000 signing bonus. Ninety seconds of discomfort, $12,000 in year one, and every future raise now compounds from 92, not 85.
If the base truly can't move

Sometimes the band is real. Then you negotiate the other levers: signing bonus, extra vacation days, remote days, a six-month review with a defined raise, education budget, start date. "If the base is fixed, is there flexibility on a signing bonus or an early review?" keeps the conversation open after the first no.

blocks.caption: a normal counter above the initial offer. High enough to matter, low enough that nobody blinks.

quiz.q: Why does a higher starting salary matter beyond year one?
options: It mostly evens out once promotions start landing
Raises are percentages of it, so the gap compounds
It changes the tax band more than the take-home pay
It matters least at firms that raise pay on a schedule
quiz.explain: Percentage raises stack on the base. A $10k higher start quietly becomes six figures of difference over a decade.

quiz.q: What actually gets offers pulled?
options: Negotiating at all, once the offer is in writing
Countering by more than about five percent
Rudeness or dishonesty, not a reasoned counter
Asking for a few days to think it over first
quiz.explain: Recruiters expect a counter; their first number is rarely the top of the band. Polite negotiation reads as competence, not greed.

quiz.q: You said your number. The recruiter goes quiet. You should…
options: Soften it, and say the current offer works too
Fill the gap with more reasons for the number
Let the silence sit: it is part of the process
Take the counter back and apologise for it
quiz.explain: Whoever fills the silence first gives ground. You made a reasonable ask; the discomfort is doing the work. Let it.

quiz.q: The recruiter says the base is truly fixed. Best response?
options: Accept it: a fixed base means the talk is finished
Ask the other levers: bonus, early review, vacation
Decline, since a firm with no flexibility says a lot
Ask them to raise it with their manager once more
quiz.explain: Base is one lever of several. Signing bonuses and defined early reviews are often easier for a company to say yes to than base changes.

cards.back: Raises compound on your starting number. One conversation can be worth $100k+ over a decade.
1) Enthusiasm. 2) "I was expecting closer to [X]." 3) One strong reason. 4) Silence.
10–15% above the offer is the normal, no-one-blinks range.
After your number, stop talking. Whoever fills the silence first loses ground.
Negotiate the other levers: signing bonus, early review with defined raise, vacation, remote days, education budget.
Rudeness and dishonesty, not polite counters. Companies expect the ask.

salary-negotiation.action: Write your four sentences for your current job or next interview, with a real number in them. Say them out loud twice: the words need to have been in your mouth before the day they matter.

index-funds-explained.hook: You already believe in index funds. You just haven't checked what your money is actually in.

blocks.text: The 13th Grade told you index funds beat stock-picking for normal people. This unit is the level-two version: what you actually own, what it silently costs, and the two or three settings that decide most of the outcome.
What you own when you own an index fund

An S&P 500 fund holds shares of the 500 largest US public companies, weighted by size. A "total market" fund holds thousands, small ones included. A "target date" fund (like Target 2065) holds a mix of stock and bond funds that automatically gets more conservative as the year approaches: the set-and-forget option inside most 401(k)s.
Fees: the quiet decider

Every fund charges an expense ratio: a yearly percentage skimmed automatically. It sounds tiny. It is not. 0.04% and 1% look similar on paper; over 30 years the difference is a six-figure haircut on a normal retirement account, taken silently, every year, regardless of performance.

blocks.caption: a fair expense ratio for a broad index fund. Big providers are at 0.02–0.10%. Anything near 1% deserves an explanation, and usually doesn't have one.

blocks.title: Real talk
blocks.text: The most expensive mistake in most 401(k)s isn't picking the wrong fund. It's never picking at all, and sitting in a high-fee default or in cash for years. Ten minutes in the settings fixes it.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: Rohan, 26, finally opens his 401(k) portal. His contributions have been sitting in a money market fund (basically cash) for two years. He moves the balance and future contributions into a Target 2065 fund with a 0.08% expense ratio. Ten minutes. Those ten minutes are plausibly worth more than every stock tip he'll ever receive.

blocks.title: The checklist for any fund
items: What does it hold? (broad index > narrow bet)
What's the expense ratio? (under 0.20% for an index fund)
Does it match your timeline? (decades away = mostly stocks; target-date funds handle this automatically)

quiz.q: A target-date fund (e.g. Target 2065)…
options: Guarantees a set amount will be there by that year
Shifts from stocks toward bonds as the date nears
Locks the money away until the year on the label
Tracks one company chosen to hold for the period
quiz.explain: It's the set-and-forget option: diversified from day one, gradually shifting toward safer holdings as retirement nears.

quiz.q: Fund A charges 0.04%, Fund B charges 1%. Over 30 years on a retirement account, the difference is roughly…
options: Small, given that both sit at or below one percent
Close to nothing once inflation is accounted for
Six figures: fees compound the way returns do
Nothing at all, if the two track the same index
quiz.explain: The percentage is skimmed yearly on the whole growing balance. Tiny-looking fee gaps become enormous over decades. Fees are the one part of investing you fully control.

quiz.q: The most expensive common 401(k) mistake is…
options: Taking the index fund over the one that is performing
Putting in more than the employer will match
Never choosing: sitting in cash or a costly default
Watching the balance closely enough to react to it
quiz.explain: Contributions parked in cash or an expensive default miss the growth entirely. Ten minutes in the portal settings is the fix.

quiz.q: A fair expense ratio for a broad index fund is…
options: Around one percent, which is the industry norm
A fifth of one percent, or lower than that
Two to three percent for the better-run funds
It hardly matters when the fund just tracks an index
quiz.explain: Major providers offer broad index funds at 0.02–0.10%. Anything approaching 1% needs a very good reason, and rarely has one.

cards.back: The yearly percentage a fund skims automatically. Under 0.20% is fair for an index fund; near 1% is a six-figure lifetime leak.

cards.front: S&P 500 fund vs total market fund
cards.back: 500 largest US companies vs. thousands of companies including small ones. Both are broad index funds; either works.
A stock/bond mix that automatically gets more conservative as your retirement year approaches. The set-and-forget 401(k) choice.
Contributions sitting in cash or a high-fee default for years because nobody picked a fund. Check the portal.
What does it hold? What does it cost (expense ratio)? Does it match my timeline?
Not returns. You control fees, contributions, and not interrupting compounding. That's most of the game.

index-funds-explained.action: Open your 401(k) or brokerage portal and find two numbers: what fund your money is in, and its expense ratio. If it's cash or above 0.5%, you found this month's highest-value ten minutes.

scam-proof.hook: Scams don't work because people are dumb. They work because the script is good, and you can learn the script.

blocks.text: Doctors, engineers, retired teachers: scam victims are disproportionately smart people who were sure it couldn't happen to them. Scams don't attack your intelligence. They attack your emotions, on a deadline.
Every scam has the same skeleton

blocks.title: The three ingredients
items: Authority: they claim to be the bank, the IRS, the police, Amazon, a government visa office, your grandchild.
Urgency: act in the next 30 minutes, your account is compromised, there's a warrant, the deal expires.
Unusual payment or access: gift cards, wire transfer, crypto, remote access to your device, or "verify" a code they sent you.

blocks.text: Any two of those together is a scam until proven otherwise. All three is a certainty. Real institutions are boring: they send letters, they wait, and they never ask for gift cards.

blocks.title: Real talk
blocks.text: The code texted to your phone is the key to your account. Anyone who asks you to read it out loud ("to verify your identity") is stealing the account while you're on the phone with them. No real company asks. Ever.
The two-step habit that beats all of them

Step one: hang up or close the message. Step two: contact the institution yourself through the number on your card or the official app. That's the entire defense. Scammers control the channel they contacted you on. A callback through an official channel breaks every script they have. The 60 seconds this takes defeats attacks that fool people with PhDs.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: "Chase fraud department" calls Nina: someone's draining her account, she must move money to a "safe account" now. Caller ID says Chase. It's spoofed. Caller ID proves nothing. Nina says "I'll call back through the app," hangs up, opens her banking app: no alerts. That's a scam defeated by a habit, not by brilliance.
The family conversation

Parents and grandparents are targeted hardest, especially in immigrant families, with scripts about visas, customs, unpaid taxes, or a relative in trouble. Agree on a family rule before it's needed: any money-moving call gets a callback through an official number, and any "family emergency" gets verified by calling that family member directly. Saying it out loud once, at dinner, is the vaccine.

blocks.caption: reported stolen by scams in the US in a single recent year, and reported is the undercount, because embarrassment keeps people quiet. Talking about scams openly is protection.

quiz.q: "Your account is compromised. Read me the code we just texted so I can verify you." This is…
options: Standard security procedure at most large banks
Safe enough, when the caller ID matches the bank
Theft in progress: that code is the key itself
Fine once they have your name and card number
quiz.explain: That code is a one-time key to log in or move money. Real institutions never ask you to read it out. Knowing your details proves nothing. Data leaks are everywhere.

quiz.q: The two-step habit that defeats nearly every scam:
options: Ask enough detailed questions to catch them out
Hang up, then call back on the official number
Keep them talking while you look the number up
Feed them wrong details and waste their time
quiz.explain: Scammers control the channel they contacted you on. A callback through an official channel (the number on your card, the real app) breaks every script.

quiz.q: Caller ID shows your bank's real name and number. This means…
options: The call is genuine and came from the bank
Nothing at all: caller ID is trivial to fake
The bank has a duty to identify itself first
Sharing details is safe on this call only
quiz.explain: Spoofing caller ID is easy and standard scam practice. Trust the callback you make, never the call you receive.

quiz.q: Authority + urgency + gift cards. How many of these does a real institution use?
options: All three, when the situation is serious enough
Urgency, though never the gift card part of it
None: real ones write letters and then wait
It varies by institution and by what is owed
quiz.explain: The IRS sends mail. Banks wait. Nobody legitimate is paid in gift cards. Pressure to act right now IS the tell.

cards.back: Authority + urgency + unusual payment/access (gift cards, wire, crypto, remote access, texted codes). Two of three = scam until proven otherwise.
1) Hang up / close it. 2) Contact the institution yourself via the official app or the number on your card. Beats every script.
One-time login keys. Anyone asking you to read one aloud is inside your account while you speak. No real company asks.
Trivially faked. Trust the call you make, never the call you receive.
Scams attack emotions on a deadline, not intelligence. Certainty that "it can't happen to me" is a vulnerability.
Money-moving calls get an official-channel callback; "family emergencies" get verified by calling that person directly. Agree on it at dinner, before it's needed.

scam-proof.action: Have the two-step conversation with one family member this week, parents first. Agree out loud: any call about money gets a hang-up and an official callback, no exceptions.
